headline: Japan Launches Historic Mission to Bring Home Samples from Mars's Moons
meta_description: Japan's MMX spacecraft successfully launched toward Mars to collect the first-ever samples from an alien moon, a five-year international effort involving NASA…
summary_short: Japan launched the MMX spacecraft on October 19th, beginning a five-year journey to collect soil samples from Mars's moon Phobos—a world first in planetary science.
body:
Japan has launched humanity's most ambitious attempt yet to retrieve material from another world's moon. On October 19th, the Martian Moons eXploration mission—MMX—lifted off from Japan's Tanegashima Space Center aboard an H3 rocket, carrying a roughly 5-ton spacecraft toward Mars. This $578 million international effort, led by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency and partnering with NASA, France's CNES, Germany's DLR, and the European Space Agency, aims to solve a decades-old mystery: how did Mars's two small, potato-shaped moons actually form?

The journey itself is only half the story. When MMX arrives at Mars in late summer 2027, it will attempt something never before accomplished—landing on Phobos, the larger of the two moons at roughly 14 miles across, to gather at least 10 grams of surface material. A French-German rover named Idefix, no larger than a microwave, will scout ahead, bouncing carefully across Phobos's extremely low gravity before the main lander touches down for just two hours to drill and collect samples using both Japanese and NASA tools.

What makes this mission scientifically thrilling is what those samples might reveal. Scientists still debate whether Phobos and its sibling Deimos were born from debris scattered by a giant Mars impact, or whether they're ancient asteroids that Mars captured long ago. Even more intriguingly, the Phobos material may contain grains blasted off Mars itself over billions of years—offering fresh clues about the Red Planet's history and the ancient conditions that might have nurtured life. After additional observations and a flyby of Deimos, MMX will depart in 2030 and return its sample capsule to Australia's desert in 2031. Beyond the science, this mission also paves the way for human Mars exploration; Phobos may one day serve as a natural staging point for astronauts heading to the Red Planet.
quick_facts: Launched October 19th from Tanegashima Space Center, Japan
Five-year, $578 million international mission with NASA, ESA, and French partners
Will land on Phobos, Mars's 14-mile-wide moon, to collect samples in 2027
Includes Idefix rover—a microwave-sized scout to navigate low gravity terrain
Sample return to Earth planned for 2031, a historic first for alien moons
